patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v1 0/2] mm: fix workingset refaults in the zswap writeback path

version_history.subject: [PATCH v1 0/2] mm: fix workingset refaults in the zswap writeback path

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 1/2] mm/swap: refault on swap-in, not in the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue where the workingset_refault function is called on every allocation in the swap cache allocator, even when it's not a refault event. The function is moved out of __swap_cache_alloc and into the callers that perform actual swap-in operations. This change ensures that refaulting is only triggered for true swap-in events, preventing incorrect counting of anon refault/activation. Additionally, the patch updates the folio_activate function to handle already-LRU folios correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/2] mm/zswap: preserve the workingset shadow across writeback
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue in the zswap compression algorithm where the workingset shadow is lost during writeback, leading to inaccurate anon refault/workingset accounting. To fix this, the patch preserves the workingset shadow within zswap by parking it in the zswap tree instead of overwriting it when a buffer folio is freed. The parked shadow is then handled at the next opportunity, whether that's through swap-in, reclaim, or slot free, ensuring accurate refault and eviction tracking.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses two issues in the zswap writeback path that cause incorrect workingset refaults. The first issue is over-counting at writeback, where a buffer folio allocated by the shrinker is counted as a refault. The second issue is lost eviction cookies at reclaim, where the original cookie is overwritten when adding the buffer to the swap cache. To fix these issues, the patch preserves the shadow within zswap itself and moves the refault evaluation out of the swap-cache allocator into the swap-in callers. This results in a significant reduction (-48% to -59%) in workingset refaults, activations, and restores, with no impact on throughput.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 0/3] mm: reject zone device folios in more folio walkers

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 0/3] mm: reject zone device folios in more folio walkers

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: skip zone device folios in madvise_free_huge_pmd()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the madvise_free_huge_pmd() function to skip zone device folios when performing lazyfree operations. The existing guards in this function do not cover all cases of zone device memory, and adding a check for zone device folios ensures that these areas are properly handled. This change addresses an issue where THP migration of zone device pages was not being filtered correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/madvise: skip zone device folios in cold/pageout PMD range
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range function, which incorrectly ages or reclaims zone device memory when it should be skipped. The issue arises from the fact that the surrounding guards do not cover all cases of zone device memory, allowing present PMDs to be aged or paged out. To fix this, the patch explicitly skips ZONE_DEVICE folios during MADV_COLD/PAGEOUT operations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/mempolicy: skip zone device folios when queueing folios
series_items.patch_summary: The patch addresses a double-put bug in the migration of zone device pages by adding an explicit check for zone device folios when queueing them. This ensures that such folios are not mistakenly added to the migration pagelist, which would lead to incorrect behavior and potential crashes.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Tested the patch series on x86_64 QEMU and reported successful results, including preventing kernel panics in a specific test case.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Aug 17, 2026 at 06:08:07PM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
>Several LRU-oriented mm walkers resolve the folio backing a PMD entry
>(or a physical pfn) and then reclaim, age, migrate, or lazyfree it
>without ever checking for ZONE_DEVICE memory.
>
>This series adds missing folio_is_zone_device() rejections, matching
>the checks that comparable walkers already perform.
>
>- mm/huge_memory, mm/madvise: the !pmd_present branch above these sites
>  only filters device-private entries (which are non-present).
>
>  A present zone device PMD (e.g. device-coherent) would still reach the
>  folio and be lazyfreed / aged / paged out. Add an explicit check.
>
>- mm/mempolicy: queue_folios_pmd() can see a present zone device PMD
>  (e.g. device-coherent) and queue it for migration.
>
>No crash reproducer - this is a correctness/hardening cleanup found by
>inspection. All checks are placed after the folio is resolved and before
>it is acted upon, on paths that already hold the relevant page-table lock,
>so no locking or refcount changes are involved.

Cool!

Gave the whole series a spin on x86_64 QEMU with a PMD-mapped
device-coherent THP. Without these patches, partial MADV_FREE and
MADV_COLD reliably hit a kernel panic in remove_migration_pte(), while
mbind(MPOL_MF_MOVE | MPOL_MF_STRICT) returned -EIO.

With v2, all three worked fine, PMD mapping stayed intact, and data
checked out :)

Note that both kernels used the same small change to the in-kernel HMM
test driver, allowing its coherent device memory to be allocated as 2 MB
folios so the PMD-mapped test case could be exercised.

Tested-by: Lance Yang <lance.yang@linux.dev>

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH 0/4] mm/mempolicy: introduce package-aware weighted interleave
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Package-aware weighted interleave patch introduces a new filtering mechanism to handle cross-socket interleave, using additional information from BIOS and node masks.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's filtering mechanism being too invasive and suggested that it should be the default weighted interleave behavior. Also questioned the usefulness of the 'package' distinction and suggested exploring abstract distance as an alternative.

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary: Addressed Gregory's concerns about the filtering mechanism and default behavior. Also discussed the use of BIOS information and abstract distance in the patch, and acknowledged the need for further discussion on the definition of package-aware weighted interleave.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, 17 Aug 2026 12:19:51 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

> The original attempt to handle cross-socket interleave tried to deal
> with this with a matrix for weights, but this was deemed too invasive.
>
> This brings back that matrix, but not for per-node weights - we're
> basically just adding an addition weighting to filter on.

Yes. It uses additional information to filter the nodes weighted
interleave selects from.

> I have some concerns with the now additional filtering mechanism
> introdced into the allocation stack, but fundamentally I think this is
> a *better* solution than a straight weight-matrix.

About the cost of the filter: when the toggle is off, the filter does
not run. When it is on, node selection needs a nodemask filtering
step, but in my tests the overhead was negligible. I will look at
this part further and check whether there is more room to optimize.

> I will need to chew on this for a bit.  It seems there's non-trivial
> sashiko bug reports here to address anyway.

I am working on the sashiko findings now. The valid ones will be
fixed in the next version.

> When worded this way, "Package" sounds completely arbitrary and not a
> useful distinction.  This really just sounds like an extention for the
> existing fallback lists to take interconnects into account.

Other reviewers also pointed out that the "package" / "socket"
terminology is ambiguous. I think the description needs a full rework
so that it explains the current state better, and I plan to do that
in the next version.

> I wonder if abstract distance either:
>   1) already gives you what you want (the secondary weight)
>   2) can be twiddled in BIOS to give you what you want.

I thought about abstract distance a lot as well. My conclusion was
that adistance alone cannot tell whether nodes are in the same
package. This is an area I am still thinking about, and it needs
more thought.

About the BIOS information: as I reported before, on the two-package
server I tested, each package had its own CXL device, but the HMAT
reported one CPU node as the initiator of both CXL nodes:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260330025914.361-1-rakie.kim@sk.com/

I will post an update on that issue as well. What this series uses
is, in the end, BIOS information too. But some of that information
has errors and some of it looks reliable, so I think we also need to
sort out which is which, and understand why.

> The way this is written it sounds to me like this should just be the
> default weighted interleave behavior.  We already know weighted
> interleave does not jive well with multi-socket systems - this just
> fixes that (in a more general sense, Socket => Package).

I agree with your point. The default is off because it was requested
during the v1 review; Jonathan asked for it:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260325123350.00004d48@huawei.com/

Enabling is also not unconditional. I added a few constraints, so it
turns on only in a specific situation: when the packages have the
same node structure. I think the definition of these on/off
conditions is open, and it needs more discussion.

Thanks again for your time and review.

Rakie Kim

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v7 0/6] fuse: add io-uring buffer pools and zero-copy

version_history.subject: [PATCH v7 0/6] fuse: add io-uring buffer pools and zero-copy

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/6] fuse: decouple fuse_ring creation from ent registration
series_items.patch_summary: This patch decouples the creation of fuse_ring from entry registration in FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) connections. The ring is now created during initialization, after a server has negotiated and set FUSE_OVER_IO_URING, rather than lazily on the first FUSE_IO_URING_CMD_REGISTER command. This change eliminates concurrent creations of the single per-connection fuse_ring, which previously required open-coded handling to detect and protect against. The patch also updates various functions to use the pre-initialized ring instead of creating it themselves.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 2/6] fuse: add FUSE_IO_URING_CMD_ADD_QUEUE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new FUSE_IO_URING_CMD_ADD_QUEUE command to the fuse-over-io-uring implementation, allowing servers to create queues explicitly and decoupling queue setup from entry registration. This is necessary for the FUSE_IO_URING_CMD_ADD_BUFPOOL command, which attaches a buffer pool to an existing queue. The patch modifies the fuse_uring_create_queue function to take an additional parameter indicating whether to fail if the queue already exists, and updates several functions to use this new command.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 3/6] fuse: add io-uring buffer pools
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new feature to the fuse io-uring implementation, allowing servers to pass in a buffer pool that can be used for servicing requests. This decouples the relationship between entries and payload buffers, enabling the kernel to optimize memory usage and reduce requirements for using fuse-over-io-uring. The server registers a buffer pool with the FUSE_IO_URING_CMD_ADD_BUFPOOL command, which is then split into individual buffers by the kernel. The kernel tracks free buffers using a bitmap and allocates them as needed for requests that require payload buffers.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 4/6] fuse: support registered buffer pools in io-uring
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for registered buffer pools in the io-uring interface of the FUSE file system. It allows servers to use a buffer pool that is also registered through io-uring, eliminating the overhead of pinning and unpining user pages per I/O request. The server can register a buffer pool by setting the FUSE_URING_REGISTERED_BUFPOOL flag when adding a bufpool, and then passing the index of the registered bufpool in every sqe submitted. This results in improved write performance, with direct-I/O throughput increasing by up to 45% compared to the baseline.

review_comments.author: Bernd Schubert
review_comments.summary: Gave Reviewed-by

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 5/6] fuse: add zero-copy over io-uring
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds zero-copy functionality to the fuse io-uring implementation, eliminating memory copies between applications, kernel, and servers for read/write operations. The server can directly access client pages or page cache folios without copying data through an intermediary buffer. Zero-copy is gated behind CAP_SYS_ADMIN and requires bufpools. The request flow involves registering relevant pages in a sparse slot of the server's io_uring registered buffer table, allowing the server to operate on these pages directly using fixed buffer operations. Non-page-backed arguments will still go through the payload buffer as normal.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 6/6] docs: fuse: document io-uring buffer pool and zero-copy uapi
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation to the Linux kernel's FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) subsystem, specifically covering its usage of io-uring buffer pools and zero-copy functionality. The new documentation explains how buffer pools decouple entries from payload buffers, allowing for more efficient memory management and reducing overhead. It also describes zero-copy, which enables servers to read from or write to client pages without an intermediary copy, requiring CAP_SYS_ADMIN privileges. This patch aims to improve the understanding of FUSE's io-uring features and their benefits.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series adds support for io-uring buffer pools and zero-copy to the FUSE file system, allowing servers to pass in a contiguous chunk of memory that the kernel can use to service requests. This reduces memory usage requirements and enables optimizations for assigning payload memory to requests. Additionally, it introduces zero-copy functionality, which allows direct access to client pages or page cache folios without copying data through an intermediary buffer, requiring CAP_SYS_ADMIN privileges and using buffer pools.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH 0/4] mm/mempolicy: introduce package-aware weighted interleave
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Package-aware weighted interleave patch introduces a new filtering mechanism to handle cross-socket interleave, using additional information from BIOS and node masks.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's filtering mechanism being too invasive and suggested that it should be the default weighted interleave behavior. Also questioned the usefulness of the 'package' distinction and suggested exploring abstract distance as an alternative.

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary: Addressed Gregory's concerns about the filtering mechanism and default behavior. Also discussed the use of BIOS information and abstract distance in the patch, and acknowledged the need for further discussion on the definition of package-aware weighted interleave.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, 17 Aug 2026 12:19:51 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

> The original attempt to handle cross-socket interleave tried to deal
> with this with a matrix for weights, but this was deemed too invasive.
>
> This brings back that matrix, but not for per-node weights - we're
> basically just adding an addition weighting to filter on.

Yes. It uses additional information to filter the nodes weighted
interleave selects from.

> I have some concerns with the now additional filtering mechanism
> introdced into the allocation stack, but fundamentally I think this is
> a *better* solution than a straight weight-matrix.

About the cost of the filter: when the toggle is off, the filter does
not run. When it is on, node selection needs a nodemask filtering
step, but in my tests the overhead was negligible. I will look at
this part further and check whether there is more room to optimize.

> I will need to chew on this for a bit.  It seems there's non-trivial
> sashiko bug reports here to address anyway.

I am working on the sashiko findings now. The valid ones will be
fixed in the next version.

> When worded this way, "Package" sounds completely arbitrary and not a
> useful distinction.  This really just sounds like an extention for the
> existing fallback lists to take interconnects into account.

Other reviewers also pointed out that the "package" / "socket"
terminology is ambiguous. I think the description needs a full rework
so that it explains the current state better, and I plan to do that
in the next version.

> I wonder if abstract distance either:
>   1) already gives you what you want (the secondary weight)
>   2) can be twiddled in BIOS to give you what you want.

I thought about abstract distance a lot as well. My conclusion was
that adistance alone cannot tell whether nodes are in the same
package. This is an area I am still thinking about, and it needs
more thought.

About the BIOS information: as I reported before, on the two-package
server I tested, each package had its own CXL device, but the HMAT
reported one CPU node as the initiator of both CXL nodes:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260330025914.361-1-rakie.kim@sk.com/

I will post an update on that issue as well. What this series uses
is, in the end, BIOS information too. But some of that information
has errors and some of it looks reliable, so I think we also need to
sort out which is which, and understand why.

> The way this is written it sounds to me like this should just be the
> default weighted interleave behavior.  We already know weighted
> interleave does not jive well with multi-socket systems - this just
> fixes that (in a more general sense, Socket => Package).

I agree with your point. The default is off because it was requested
during the v1 review; Jonathan asked for it:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260325123350.00004d48@huawei.com/

Enabling is also not unconditional. I added a few constraints, so it
turns on only in a specific situation: when the packages have the
same node structure. I think the definition of these on/off
conditions is open, and it needs more discussion.

Thanks again for your time and review.

Rakie Kim

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] mm: memcg: flush empty per-cpu stock slots on memcg offlining
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch aims to flush empty per-cpu stock slots on memcg offlining, addressing potential cache misses and improving performance.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the patch's potential to cause cache misses due to unnecessary drain operations. Suggested an alternative solution using a conditional check for memcg descendants and dying objects.

review_comments.author: Song Hu
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged Joshua's concerns and agreed to drop the disputed claim about objcg symmetry. Confirmed that the ordering of CSS_DYING and css_offline ensures correct behavior.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi, 

\u5728 2026/8/17 12:30, Joshua Hahn \u5199\u9053:
> On Mon, 17 Aug 2026 10:59:17 +0800 Song Hu <husong@kylinos.cn> wrote:
> 
>> refill_stock() takes a css reference for each cached memcg slot and
>> mem_cgroup_css_offline() relies on drain_all_stock() to release those
>> references before the cgroup can finish dying.
>>
>> consume_stock() can drive a slot's nr_pages to zero while its cached[]
>> pointer stays set.  is_memcg_drain_needed() skips such empty slots, so
>> the offlining drain is a no-op for them: the pinned css reference is
>> released only if the slot happens to be evicted by later unrelated
>> charges on the same CPU, or by CPU hotplug.  The memcg then lingers
>> in the dying state indefinitely.  On a CPU with container churn, a
>> per-cpu stock can pin up to NR_MEMCG_STOCK (7) zombie memcgs.
>>
>> The sibling obj_stock_flush_required() has no such gate: a cached
>> objcgs slot is flushed regardless of its byte count.  Drop the
>> nr_pages gate from is_memcg_drain_needed() accordingly.  Draining an
>> empty slot is a single css_put() and a NULL store, and it happens at
>> most once per slot per drain, so the extra work is negligible.
> 
> Hi Song,
> 
> I feel that this above statement is quite misleading.
> Scheduling a drain on a memcg that doesn't have stock eventually
> performs a drain operation on every memcg cached in that CPU.
> 
Right, I missed that drain_local_memcg_stock() flushes the whole
stock, so an unrelated charge below a dying memcg would throw away the
other slots on that CPU.  Will drop that claim and the objcg
comparison from the changelog; the objcg side has no reference to
release from the stock, so there is no symmetry to argue from.

> drain_local_memcg_stock
>   drain_stock_fully
>   {
>     for (i = 0; i < NR_MEMCG_STOCK; ++i)
>       drain_stock(stock, i);
>   {
> 
> Sure, for any empty stock during this iteration drain_stock is trivial,
> but for nonempty stock that happen to co-exist on the CPU, it's forcing
> a cache miss on the next charge.
> 
> The problem that you note does seem quite real though. I think a less
> invasive solution could be something like
> 
> if (mem_cgroup_is_descendant(memcg, root_memct) &&
>     (READ_ONCE(stock->nr_pages[i]) || css_is_dying(&memcg->css))
> 
Will do.  The ordering works out: kill_css_sync() sets CSS_DYING
before css_offline is queued, so css_is_dying() is already true when
mem_cgroup_css_offline() calls drain_all_stock().
> By the way, I think the argument that "obj_stock_flush_required has no
> such gate so is_memcg_drain_needed doesn't need one too" is also not
> really correct since a dying objcg doesn't flush anyways. 
> 
Thanks,
Song> I hope you have a great day,
> Joshua
> 
>> This is easily reproduced with short-lived cgroups pinned to one CPU:
>> 12 charge/exit/rmdir cycles leave nr_dying_subsys_memory at +2, stable
>> across later slot displacement.
>>
>> Fixes: d1a05b6973c7 ("memcg: do not try to drain per-cpu caches without pages")
>> Signed-off-by: Song Hu <husong@kylinos.cn>
>> ---
>>  mm/memcontrol.c | 8 ++++++--
>>  1 file changed, 6 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
>>
>> diff --git a/mm/memcontrol.c b/mm/memcontrol.c
>> index 17da1f43b7d3..b931ec16bb82 100644
>> --- a/mm/memcontrol.c
>> +++ b/mm/memcontrol.c
>> @@ -2291,8 +2291,12 @@ static bool is_memcg_drain_needed(struct memcg_stock_pcp *stock,
>>  		if (!memcg)
>>  			continue;
>>  
>> -		if (READ_ONCE(stock->nr_pages[i]) &&
>> -		    mem_cgroup_is_descendant(memcg, root_memcg)) {
>> +		/*
>> +		 * An empty slot still pins a css reference which
>> +		 * mem_cgroup_css_offline() relies on drain_all_stock()
>> +		 * to release.
>> +		 */
>> +		if (mem_cgroup_is_descendant(memcg, root_memcg)) {
>>  			flush = true;
>>  			break;
>>  		}
>> -- 
>> 2.43.0
